title: Spring Lecture #28: Hibernate Fundamentals with Spring Boot

questions.question: The lecture's repository injects a `jakarta.persistence.EntityManager`, and the project uses `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa`. How are Jakarta Persistence (JPA) and Hibernate related?
options: Hibernate is the specification and JPA is one of its implementations, like EclipseLink
JPA defines the API (`@Entity`, `EntityManager`, …) and Hibernate is a provider that implements it; at runtime the `EntityManager` is backed by Hibernate
JPA and Hibernate are two unrelated libraries, and the starter makes you choose one at startup
JPA replaces JDBC entirely, so Hibernate no longer needs a JDBC driver or `DataSource`
questions.explanation: Jakarta Persistence is a specification of contracts. Hibernate is an implementation (the provider Spring Boot uses by default), much like `List` and `ArrayList`. Hibernate still sits on top of JDBC, so it needs the MySQL driver and the `DataSource` configured from `spring.datasource.*`.
questions.source: notes: Introduction to Hibernate / JPA as a specification

questions.question: A team deployed with `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create` to a shared test MySQL database. After every restart, all previously inserted students are gone. Which setting stops this while still letting Hibernate check that the entities match the existing tables?
options: `create-drop`, because it only drops tables on shutdown, not on startup
`update`, because it recreates the tables only when the mapping changes
`none`, because it validates the schema without changing it
`validate`, because it compares the mappings with the schema and never creates or modifies tables
questions.explanation: `create` drops and recreates the mapped schema at startup, which wipes the data. `validate` only checks that the schema matches and fails fast if it doesn't, without touching the tables. `create-drop` also recreates the schema at startup (and drops it at shutdown), and `none` does no checking at all. In production, schema changes are usually managed with Flyway or Liquibase.
questions.source: notes: Schema generation with ddl-auto; code: application.properties

questions.question: With Spring Boot's default naming strategy and `ddl-auto=update`, what does Hibernate generate for this mapping (the lecture's `Address` embeddable embedded once)?
options: One `students` table with columns id, student_name, email, age, house_no, street, city, state, pincode
A `students` table plus a separate `address` table with a `student_id` foreign key
A `students` table whose `address` column stores the serialized `Address` object
One `students` table, but the Address columns are prefixed: address_house_no, address_street, address_city, address_state, address_pincode
questions.explanation: An `@Embeddable` has no identity or table of its own; its fields are flattened into the owner's table. Spring Boot's default naming turns `houseNo` into `house_no`, and `@Column(name = "student_name")` renames the `name` column. Prefixes appear only if you add them with `@AttributeOverride`, and a separate table is what `@ElementCollection` would create.

questions.question: `private StudentStatus status;` was mapped WITHOUT `@Enumerated`, and thousands of rows exist. A developer adds a new constant at the top: `enum StudentStatus { PENDING, ACTIVE, INACTIVE, SUSPENDED }`. Suddenly, students who were ACTIVE show as PENDING. Why, and what is the right mapping?
options: `ddl-auto=update` rewrote the status column when the enum changed; switching to `validate` fixes it
Hibernate caches enum values from the first startup; clearing the second-level cache fixes it
Without `@Enumerated`, enums are stored by ORDINAL (position), so old value 0 now means PENDING; `@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)` stores the constant name and avoids this
Enum fields must be `String` in the entity; Hibernate cannot map enums directly
questions.explanation: JPA's default enum mapping is `EnumType.ORDINAL`, which stores the constant's position. Inserting or reordering constants silently changes the meaning of existing numbers. The lecture uses `@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)`, which stores readable values like ACTIVE that stay stable when constants are added. (Existing ordinal data would still need a migration.)
questions.source: notes: Enum mapping; code: StudentStatus.java, Student.java (commented status field)

questions.question: Students belong to a department that is shared by many students, has its own head, and is often queried and updated on its own. How should `Department` be modelled relative to `Student`?
options: As an `@Embeddable` inside `Student`, because it is part of the student's data
As an `@ElementCollection` of Strings in `Student`, so that each student keeps its own department names
As its own `@Entity` with an `@Id`, because it has an independent identity and lifecycle and is shared
As a `@Transient` field, because department data should not be persisted with the student
questions.explanation: Entities have their own identity and lifecycle and can be shared and queried independently. Value types (embeddables, element collections) are owned by one entity, have no `@Id`, and cannot be fetched with `find()`. Embedding a shared department would copy its data into every student row, so updates would have to touch every copy.
questions.source: notes: Entity types versus value types; Entity association versus embedded value

questions.question: `private Boolean isMonitor;` is mapped with `@Convert(converter = BooleanToStringConverter.class)` (the lecture's converter). A DBA manually inserted one row with `is_monitor = 'yes'` (lowercase). What does `isMonitor` contain when that row is loaded, and what is written for a student whose `isMonitor` is `null`?
options: `true`, and the string "No" is written for `null`
`false`, because `"Yes".equals("yes")` is case-sensitive; SQL NULL is written for `null`
`true`, because Hibernate lower-cases values before calling the converter; SQL NULL is written for `null`
A `ConversionException`, because 'yes' is neither "Yes" nor "No"
questions.explanation: Hibernate passes the column value to `convertToEntityAttribute` unchanged, and `String.equals` is case-sensitive, so 'yes' becomes `false`, a silent data bug. For writes, the converter's explicit null check returns `null`, so SQL NULL is stored. The converter never throws for unknown values; anything other than "Yes" simply maps to false.

questions.question: A developer uncomments both `Address` fields in the lecture's `Student` but deletes the `@AttributeOverrides` blocks, leaving the code below. What happens at startup with `ddl-auto=update`?
options: Hibernate fails to build the mapping because both embeddings map to the same columns (house_no, street, city, …), a repeated/duplicated column error
Hibernate automatically prefixes the columns with the field names (current_address_city, permanent_address_city, …)
It starts, and both addresses share the same columns, so saving one address overwrites the other
Hibernate stores the second address in a separate `permanent_address` table
questions.explanation: Each `@Embedded Address` contributes the same column names by default, so the entity ends up with duplicate column mappings and Hibernate rejects it when building the metadata. `@AttributeOverride` exists to give each embedding location its own column names (current_city vs parmanent_city in the lecture code). Default naming does not add prefixes automatically.
questions.source: notes: Multiple embedded objects / @AttributeOverride; code: Student.java (commented block)

questions.question: The entity uses `@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)` with MySQL, and `spring.jpa.show-sql=true`. What is printed, in order, when this service method runs inside one transaction (first student in an empty table)?
options: Before: null, After: null, and then the INSERT SQL at commit, because SQL is always deferred until flush
The INSERT SQL first, then Before: 1, After: 1, because `new` reserves an id from the database
Before: null, After: null, and no INSERT, because `persist()` without `save()` never writes
Before: null, then the INSERT SQL, then After: 1, because an IDENTITY id is only known after the database executes the INSERT, so Hibernate runs it during `persist()`
questions.explanation: With IDENTITY, the database generates the key during the INSERT. Hibernate needs the id immediately to register the managed entity, so it executes the INSERT at `persist()` time instead of waiting for flush/commit, and the id is populated right after. A new object has a null id before `persist()`. (This is also why IDENTITY prevents JDBC batching of inserts.)
questions.source: notes: 5.2 Create with persist(); code: StudentRepository.save()

questions.question: The `students` table already holds data in a `student_name` column. A developer changes the mapping from `@Column(name = "student_name", length = 100)` to `@Column(name = "full_name", length = 100)` and restarts with `ddl-auto=update`. What is the result?
options: Hibernate renames `student_name` to `full_name`, keeping all existing data
Hibernate adds a new `full_name` column; `student_name` stays with the old data but is no longer mapped, so existing students load with a null name
Startup fails, because `update` refuses to run when a mapped column is missing
Hibernate drops `student_name` and creates `full_name`, so all existing names are lost but no data is duplicated
questions.explanation: `update` only tries to ADD what is missing (tables, columns); it cannot know that a mapping was renamed, and it does not drop or rename existing columns. The old data stays in `student_name` while the entity reads the empty `full_name`. This is why the notes warn that `update` is not a production migration tool and recommend Flyway or Liquibase for renames.

questions.question: A field is mapped as `@Column(precision = 5, scale = 2) private BigDecimal percentage;`. Which value can NOT be stored in the generated column?
questions.explanation: Precision is the total number of digits and scale is the number after the decimal point, so DECIMAL(5,2) allows 3 integer digits: the maximum is 999.99. 1000.00 needs 4 integer digits (6 in total) and is out of range. 98.75 (precision 4) and 0.5 (stored as 0.50) fit. `BigDecimal` is used instead of `double` so these decimal values stay exact.
